articles.title_orig: ‘They Never Stop’: Taipei Mayoral Candidate Puma Shen on Fighting Chinese Cognitive Warfare
articles.title_zh: ‘They Never Stop’: Taipei Mayoral Candidate Puma Shen on Fighting Chinese Cognitive Warfare
articles.content_orig:
Puma Shen, the Democratic Progressive Party’s candidate for Taipei mayor, speaks at a campaign event in Taipei’s Guandu neighborhood on Nov. 15, 2026.
The legislative office of Puma Shen feels more like a college dorm than a lawmaker’s workplace. Every surface is piled high with anime figurines, camping equipment, and baseball memorabilia. “I don’t have enough space at home, so I have to put it all in my office,” he tells TIME. “Otherwise, my wife will be p—d off!”
Read more: How Taiwan Is Turning Tech Supremacy Into a Security Shield
Then the décor turns political. A large Ukrainian flag, signed by troops during Shen’s 2023 visit, hangs on one wall. On the door, a piece of Chinese calligraphy reads “Die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist”—a designation Beijing applied to him that has become a point of pride. “On the first day when I was sanctioned by China, my colleague actually gave this to me,” grins Shen, 44.
It’s a sanction that illustrates Shen’s position in Taiwan politics, where fault lines are increasingly drawn between competing visions for preserving the self-ruling island’s autonomy. Beijing claims sovereignty over Taiwan and has not ruled out using force to achieve “reunification.” Shen’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) sees security in forging a path distinct from Beijing; the opposition Nationalists (KMT), meanwhile, believe building bridges with China better serves the islanders' interests.
On Nov. 28, Taiwan is holding local elections that will serve as a bellwether of the national mood, and Shen is hoping to unseat the KMT incumbent Chiang Wan-an for the prestigious post of Taipei mayor, often a steppingstone to the presidency.
Besides serving as a lawmaker, Shen is also an associate professor of criminology at National Taipei University and in 2019 co-founded Doublethink Lab, a civil society research group that tracks disinformation, cognitive warfare, and digital authoritarianism.
The following has been edited for clarity and length.
TIME: You're standing as the DPP candidate for Taipei mayor. What is the number one problem Taipei faces that you want to fix?
City-level issues, for instance, like transportation, or making sure that streets are clean, [are important]. But I also care about resilience, I care about prosperity, and I think prosperity and resilience are actually the same thing, because the city can only be prosperous in the long run if it can hold together when anything happens.
So it's not just about infrastructure; the connections within neighborhoods, connection within the community, is still the most important thing here in Taipei. I think loneliness is a very urban issue. So, to solve loneliness, to actually build up connections within the community, can contribute to resilience.
When people get to know each other, they know when something happened, who is not able to get down the stairs, they know which door to knock on if something happens. That's the thing that I really want to build in our city.
You've argued that China's influence operations against Taiwan are already a form of cognitive warfare. What does that look like in everyday Taiwanese life?
It's not just crude propaganda; it's more about how our daily life might be infiltrated by their information. They can have lively videos talking about cute animals or fortune telling, and so it's very easy for the younger generation to consume that kind of information. But if you click then you're pushed into videos talking about how the U.S. cannot be trusted, Japan is not your friend, and the E.U. is too far away, trying to imply that China is your only friend. It is not just the younger generation, but also elderly people, who are watching all these videos online and could be influenced by all this disinformation.
Taiwan is a proudly open society. How do you guard against manipulation while still allowing for a free media landscape and avoiding censorship?
There are so many ways that you can stop information manipulation. One thing is just to cut off the source, but I don't think it's a good idea. We're an open society, we're a democratic society. You're allowed to consume any kind of information that you like.
Another way is that you try to regulate the social media platform; for example, identification to make sure that there's not so many fake accounts controlled by just one guy, allowing real voices to be disseminated. But I think the best way is still through education, because it's more difficult for them to infiltrate offline.
So, if people are hanging out with each other and discussing conspiracies they saw online, that's the gist of democracy and the best way we can counter information operations.
Some analysts suggest there are thousands of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) operatives in Taiwan. Do you agree with these reports?
For me, it's more about risk management, because let's say businessmen or singers and actors travel to China often. But they're victims, because when they have their business interests over there, they could be threatened by China. We know these guys are traveling to China; they might meet someone from the United Front [CCP overseas influence department] and they need to be protected. It's not like, “hey, they're traveling over there and when they come back we treat them like a spy.” I don't think it's a good idea.
For us, it's all about transparency, and our policy is that when [officials] want to travel to China, you need to report, and the government will tell you, “hey, these are the guys that maybe you don't want to meet,” or if they threaten you, what you could do. In that way, you're protecting your citizens instead of labeling them as “infiltrated by China” so we need to investigate. I don't think it's a good idea to do that.
How vulnerable is Taiwan today to Chinese political influence through business, media, entertainment?
I think media is pretty much the same [as business], because most media are invested by entrepreneurs, and lots have their business in China. So, once you have the business interest there, you might be asked by the Chinese agent, “hey, maybe you should put on some political talk show and try to denounce the current government.” There are journalists being investigated for this kind of situation. So, it's all about how we can protect them at the very beginning instead of punishing them afterwards. Risk management is always a better idea in democratic society.
You've been personally sanctioned by China. How has that changed your understanding of the threat?
When we talk about information operations, it could be online activities. The other thing is offline activities; if someone has been proactively approached by China, which may ask him to do something. But to politicians or to the military, it's called psychological warfare. They want to put pressure on you and make sure that you make wrong decisions. So, they sanction me and try to say, “hey, if you travel abroad, I will arrest you.” However, because I’ve got a public profile it's much easier for me to deal with that pressure. But there are the other guys who do not [have such a profile]: the Uyghurs , or the Hong Kong dissidents . All these guys are facing the same pressure.
So, the first thing is that we need to unify. And second is to show we're not afraid. When they said they want to arrest me if I travel abroad, only two days later I traveled to Germany, the Netherlands, and France, because I want to prove that it's not a real thing. That's the spirit I also want to show to Taiwanese people but also other people all around the world that have been sanctioned or threatened by China.
You mentioned some European countries, but would you still feel secure traveling to places more in Beijing's orbit, such as Thailand or Cambodia?
Thailand, Cambodia, maybe Malaysia—they all have a record that they send human rights defenders or dissidents back to China, so it's not really safe to travel.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s DoJ ‘looked into’ concerns about Huang after affair with suspected Chinese spy but says no security risk found – live
articles.title_zh: Trump’s DoJ ‘looked into’ concerns about Huang after affair with suspected Chinese spy but says no security risk found – live
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

In fact, the longer you do, the more likely it is for something on your wish list to sell out. Start browsing sales at Amazon , Walmart , Home Depot , Apple , PlayStation , Alo , Hoka , Nintendo and more as soon as possible — at this point, you can be pretty confident that live discounts are as good as they’re going to get.
I’ve covered major sales events as a reporter and on-air correspondent for NBC Selected since 2020. Hoka made minimal changes between the models, so it’s worth buying the Arahi 8 if you need a solid walking or running shoe . It has a built-in stability system that helps prevent overpronation, and a moderate layer of soft cushioning to absorb shock and keep your feet comfortable. The sneakers come in regular and wide styles, and men’s and women’s sizes.

It picks up dirt, hair and crumbs while scrubbing floors to leave them sparkling — and the best part is that you don’t have to lift a finger. When the robot is done cleaning, it returns to its charging base and empties itself into the dustbag. It maps your home to detect where carpets, hard floors and obstacles are, and connects to an app that lets you set schedules and routines, as well as adjust settings.
Batteries are an essential you always need to have at home, so you may as well buy them on sale, especially before the holidays — in my family, they’re always in high demand to power remotes, lights and toys. This pack comes with 48 total: 24 AA and 24 AAA . The batteries hold their power for up to 10 years in storage and they’re leak-resistant for up to two years, according to the brand.
If you’re not a smartwatch person but want to track health metrics, try the Oura Ring 5 , which is the brand’s smallest, most low-profile device yet. It has sensors on the inside that detect your pulse, letting it collect insights about your sleep, workouts, heart rate, stress levels and more. All the data it collects gets stored in the Oura app, where you also get a daily readiness score. The Oura Ring is water- and scratch-resistant, and a full battery lasts for about a week. Note: a $5.99 per month Oura membership , sold separately, is required for use, but you get a one-month membership free with your purchase.
You’ll always find at least one person wearing these retro over-ear headphones at NBC Selected’s office. You can choose from four noise-cancellation levels depending on how well you want to hear the world around you, and take calls while wearing them thanks to built-in microphones. The headphones have multiple buttons on them that let you adjust the volume, shuffle through tracks and engage a voice assistant, as well as control your connected device’s camera. A full battery gives you up to 135 hours of battery life, according to the brand.
The spherical shape of Wonderboom’s portable Bluetooth speaker gives you 360-degree sound, and a full battery lasts for up to 14 hours, according to the brand. It also floats and is water-resistant, so you can use it in the pool, at the beach or while taking a bath. The speaker has outdoor boost and podcast modes to enhance audio as needed, and there’s a loop on the top, which you can add a carabiner clip to and attach it to your bag, bike or lounge chair.
Once you plug this Bluetooth transmitter into the headphone jack on an airplane seat, gaming console or exercise machine, it streams audio to your wireless headphones. The AirFly pairs with up to two headphones at a time, and it gives you over 25 hours of battery life on a full battery.

You can quickly turn the brushroll on and off depending on what type of floors you’re cleaning, and detach the pod to tackle hard to reach areas like stairs and furniture. The pod has a long hose and you interchangeable attachments: a dusting brush and a crevice tool.

It comes with a snow-covered tree stump and spruce tree stand, letting you display the fox in its habitat. The red fox is moderately challenging and best for those 9 years old and up.

articles.title_orig: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Ferrari’s new 296 Challenge Stradale is a badass, 670-horsepower, non-hybrid race car for the road. Want one? It’ll cost you around $307,000 before options.
But if you want to get a little fancier with your new Ferrari, the automaker’s online configurator has plenty of ways to customize the supercar. And some of them are pretty wild. I wasted 30 minutes of my day dialing in my perfect 296 CS.
Let’s start with the most important part: paint. Ferrari offers a whopping 35 colors, split into four categories: Standard, Historical, Classic, and Special. You could go with the classic Rosso Corsa or Giallo Modena, but I'm going with something a little different here: Giallo Ambra, aka fancy orange.
Once you pick your paint, Ferrari lets you choose from a handful of livery options, including upper- and lower-body graphics, wing decals, door numbers, and more. Normally, I'd say a livery is mandatory on a car like this. But the 296 Challenge Stradale looks so damn good in a single color that it really doesn't need one.
Ferrari also lets you turn just about anything into carbon fiber. Front splitter? Carbon fiber. Rear diffuser? Carbon fiber. Even the engine covers? That's right, carbon fiber.
If you really want to go crazy, you can replace all the glass with Lexan, a lightweight polycarbonate that's a little lighter than traditional glass. That should help shave off a few pounds. Ferrari will even let you ditch the Prancing Horse badges on the front fenders entirely or swap the metal logos for painted ones.
Ferrari offers six wheel designs for the 296 CS, ranging from light silver to darker gray and black. You can also customize the wheel bolts, center caps, and more. I'm going with Forged Diamond-Polished wheels and titanium wheel bolts.
Depending on how you plan to use your 296 (primarily on road or track), Ferrari offers both Bridgestone and Pirelli tires. There are even two Pirelli "Color Edition" options with yellow or gray accents. We'll pass on those.
Brake calipers are available in eight different colors, ranging from black and red to yellow and silver.
Most of the interior upgrades are pretty subtle. You can choose floor mats with or without logos, pick from 26 stitching colors (we went with Filo Spec Flash Orange to match the exterior), and customize the lower portion of the dashboard with 22 different colors.
Perhaps the most important choice, though, is the seats. Ferrari offers two options: Racing and "Best Weight," as the automaker calls it. The racing seats appear to be lighter and probably less comfortable, but Ferrari doesn't really divulge any specifics.
There are seven different Alcantara colors available, depending on which seats you choose. You can also customize the seatbelts with six different colors, add a central racing stripe, and choose from additional stitching options.
Like most Ferraris, the 296 CS doesn't have a dedicated center touchscreen. That said, Ferrari does offer an optional passenger display, which seems a little odd in a car like this. Maybe your nephew can watch Shrek while you lap COTA. The world is your oyster.
As you'd expect, Ferrari doesn't list prices for any of these options in its configurator. You'll have to contact your local dealer to find out how much any of them will set you back.
But getting into a new 296 Challenge Stradale will cost you at least $307,000 to start. And that's before you start checking boxes.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela moves toward possible debt restructuring with release of economic framework
articles.title_zh: Venezuela moves toward possible debt restructuring with release of economic framework
articles.content_orig:
Joseph Cotterill and Joe Daniels in London
Published November 24 2026
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Venezuela has unveiled debts of close to $240bn, as Delcy Rodríguez’s US-backed government published an economic framework for the biggest sovereign debt restructuring in history.
The South American nation’s finance ministry published up-to-date economic data for the first time in years on Tuesday, as the long-delayed anchor for what it said was a “clear and credible” plan to reduce the country’s debts and revive access to international markets following the US’s overthrow of president Nicolás Maduro in January.
Venezuela defaulted in 2017 after years of economic mismanagement, falling oil production and US sanctions that finally cut off payments and made a restructuring impossible for years.
Rodríguez’s government in May said it had hired a US adviser, Centerview Partners, to work on a restructuring, starting with an updated “macroeconomic framework” to guide talks. Venezuela is yet to release a full debt sustainability analysis on the scope for a restructuring.
Prices of bonds issued by the government and Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state oil company, rose about 2 cents to 3 cents on the dollar on Tuesday. The debts have gained about 70 per cent in price this year but trade at between a third and half of their face value.
Tuesday’s report said: “Venezuela’s public debt is in a state of protracted default and is unsustainable, reflecting the constraints imposed by financial sanctions, the decline in hydrocarbon revenues and years of macroeconomic imbalances.”
The FT in June reported the country was set to reveal a $240bn debt pile that was much larger than market estimates of less than $200bn. Tuesday’s report shows the difference largely consists of “non-financial” debts owed by PDVSA.
Preparations for a restructuring were delayed by the devastating earthquake that hit Caracas in June, people familiar with the matter said.
The figures released on Tuesday shine the most detailed light on the economy’s performance in the period since Maduro’s removal, which has included a US-backed investor rush for oil deals and the quake’s devastating impact.
The economy is set to grow 5 per cent this year, less than last year. Inflation is “exceptionally high” and is set to end 2026 at an annual rate of more than 300 per cent. It is forecast to fall to 72 per cent next year, according to the document.
Venezuela’s economy is seen doubling in size to $200bn by 2031 from less than $100bn just before Maduro’s ousting. This would be roughly half the size of the country’s peak GDP in 2012, in the last years of the rule of the late leader Hugo Chávez.
The small size of the economy and the resulting very high ratio of debt to GDP mean most bondholders expect to swallow a large reduction in the face value of their claims. However, they say the value of the restructured debt will depend almost entirely on how quickly the country can raise oil production and revenues.
Tuesday’s document forecasts PDVSA and international partners will spend about $160bn on oil projects over the next decade, with just under half coming from the state oil company.
Of a combined $237.5bn in debt owed by Venezuela and PDVSA at the end of last year, nearly half is made up of $110bn in defaulted bonds and years of unpaid interest.
The country also owes $6bn in bank loans and more than $26bn in arbitration awards — international legal claims that largely involve oil majors and miners whose assets were expropriated under Chávez.
China makes up nearly $17bn of $23bn in debt that Venezuela owes to official creditors, with $5bn owed to Russia. Just over $4bn is owed to multilateral creditors such as development banks.
The finance ministry said it had also identified $67bn in “non-financial obligations . . . entirely concentrated at the PDVSA level”, including $17bn owed to suppliers and $10bn related to joint ventures in oil projects. About $30bn of these debts are classed as “intra-public sector” obligations.
“These liabilities add an additional layer of complexity to the overall debt profile and underline the importance of a comprehensive approach when assessing the perimeter and dynamics of public sector indebtedness,” the report said.
Unusually for such a large restructuring, the IMF has not played its traditional role of leading the analysis of debt sustainability, despite Venezuela resuming ties with the fund this year.
Many investors and experts want the fund to be more involved. Some have questioned whether a deal on a debt workout is viable before elections, which US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said will “ideally” be held next year.
The Latin American Committee on Macroeconomic and Financial Issues, a regional group of independent economists, this month said Venezuela should hold elections and allow the IMF to conduct its own analysis before proceeding with any restructuring.

articles.title_orig: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.title_zh: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.content_orig:
Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy in which he saw visions of the devil and hell while struggling with how to exercise power, newly published diaries of the late pontiff reveal.
The Argentine pope intermittently kept a diary between 1992 and 2024, first during his time as a bishop in Argentina and then following his election as pope. Now, several of those entries have been compiled in a book published on Tuesday. It was written by Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, one of Francis’ closest aides and a fellow Argentine, who offers a detailed commentary on the papal diaries.
The 160-page “The Private Diary of Pope Francis” is focused primarily on the pope’s spiritual life and pastoral agenda, although it also details how the first Latin American pope struggled with temptations connected to the use of power in 2021-2022. It also includes what the pope describes as encounters with the devil along with his thoughts about his successor, Leo XIV, whom he characterized as “irreproachable.”
The publication of papal diaries is rare, but not unprecedented, and can provide unusually personal insights. While some popes order that their personal papers be destroyed, the diaries of John XXIII were published posthumously, as were some papers of John Paul II.
Francis wrote 86 pages of the black-covered diary — initially a planner for the year 1992 — while he was in Argentina and 55 pages while he was pope. “He showed me a few books, including what looked like an old agenda book with a leather cover. When he opened it, I saw that it was filled with notes in his handwriting. He told me, ‘From this, you will all see,’” Fernández wrote.
Here are some of the major revelations:
The diaries say that the pope experienced “frequent demonic attacks,” and Francis details three encounters with the devil: two while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires and another in 2018, when he was pope. Francis wrote that the devil has “eyes of fire,” also describing them as “menacing” and “seductive” eyes.
“I can’t forget his eyes the first two times — from the car when I was returning to the house, and in the choir loft during Mass. However, he always reappears in different situations,” the pope wrote in an entry for August 18, 2024. The third occasion came after returning from a visit to Chile in 2018, a trip overshadowed by the clerical sexual abuse scandal.
“On one occasion, a few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice [his underlining], triumphant, possessing everything: ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted,’” the pope wrote on January 24, 2021. “Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice. The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me.”
Catholic teaching holds that the devil is a fallen angel and a real presence, and Catholic tradition cautions that those who are serious about attaining holiness will often encounter strong spiritual opposition. During his pontificate, Francis would frequently mention the devil, linking it to gossip and money. “The devil enters through the pockets,” he often said.
The diary also includes details of how Francis believed God spoke to him in dreams. On one occasion, Francis recounted seeing “the entrance to hell.” The pope, in 2018, described it as a form of “pagan seduction in full force,” an apparent reference to the worshipping of idols. “I peeked in to look a little and it terrified me. It was before going to sleep. I grabbed the rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help,” he wrote.
The book reveals that in 2021-2022, Francis underwent a spiritual crisis connected to a temptation or “curiosity” with power and which was partly connected to excessive activity and feelings of self-sufficiency. It was, the pope explained, also linked to “governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”
To counter the temptation, he sought to exercise greater humility and patience, even leaving people in place in the church’s central administration who others felt were undermining his papacy. During his 12-year pontificate, Francis, initiated several reforms in the church, including on the treatment of LGBTQ Catholics and the role of women, but faced significant opposition. Some of it came from inside the Vatican, where some bishops and cardinals openly resisted his reforms.
The Pope Francis I knew: Reflections from CNN’s Vatican correspondent
“One time in my presence, a bishop asked him why he had not yet fired someone in the Roman Curia who had been speaking badly of him in public and pursuing a personal agenda very different than his,” wrote Cardinal Fernández, who was appointed by Francis to lead the Vatican’s doctrine office. “After an interminable silence, he responded by explaining that he felt a strong sensation in his heart that God did not want him to become a puppeteer who uses and manipulates people according to his own convenience. He explained that, for this reason, he preferred to let that person remain in his position.”
While the diary doesn’t go into specific examples, the pope wrote on December 30, 2022, that he refused the temptation to treat “others like puppets.” In 2018, he said that “this sense of self-sufficiency and I can solve everything brought me to the gates of hell. I can’t forget the day I saw it.”
The crisis that Francis underwent, Fernández explained, was “connected to power” and the curiosity to “discover what it is like to exercise one’s own power.” As a member of the Jesuit religious order, the pope was continuously engaged in a spiritual discernment, essentially engaging in self-examination to determine whether he was working for self-interest or the good of others.
For Francis, feeling that he was “above the world” through his power was “the path of the worst spiritual worldliness imaginable, which he sought to dismantle by avoiding every symbol or expression of papal ‘majesty’ or ‘glory,’” Fernández added.
During his pontificate, Francis adopted a simple style, living in a Vatican guesthouse, wearing black orthopedic shoes and refusing certain papal vestments.
While the diaries focus on the pope’s spiritual life, they do include comments about the clerical sexual abuse crisis, including in Chile in 2018. At the time, Francis was criticized for dismissing the case of a bishop who had been accused of witnessing and covering up abuse when he was a priest. The pope later apologized for his handling of the case and summoned all the bishops from the country to Rome. In an unprecedented move, the bishops offered their resignations to the pope en masse .
“Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane. I fell off the cot then,” Francis wrote. “It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn’t think it was so serious.” The phrase “fell off the cot,” the book explains, means to suddenly wake up to something. Francis would go on to make several reforms aimed at tackling clerical sexual abuse.
Examine the power held by popes throughout history
The diaries reveal the pope’s thoughts on Cardinal Robert Prevost, the future Pope Leo XIV, whom Francis brought to the Vatican to lead the department for appointing bishops. According to Fernández, Francis called Prevost “a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man.”
He was also generous to his critics, including Cardinals Robert Sarah, a Guinean, and Gerhard Muller, a German prelate. The Argentine pontiff said Sarah had “a refined spiritual sensitivity” and that Muller “seems aggressive but he’s a good man,” Fernández wrote.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.content_orig:
Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.
That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation.
Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone.
Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout.
Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad , and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast.
Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision.
The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland , hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members.
The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics , and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries.
The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock.
The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons.
Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice.
What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward.
Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to ) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it.
Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back , and make any possibility of compromise seem remote.
There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties.
Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins.
But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not.
Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines.
The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing.
This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow up 400 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq in retreat a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap: live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow up 400 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq in retreat a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap: live updates
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether it was being investigated by the administration.
Blanche said he had no information about Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement as the AI microchip maker's chief executive.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned over his relationship with a former executive for Megaspeed - the alleged China spy - due to national security concerns.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist tech company Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer that has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen."
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that that the president is saying to the American people ... It shouldn't be what my message would be either," Blanche said.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down more than 7% in early afternoon trading, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's return was announced.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.
Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees and Says He Is in Therapy
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees and Says He Is in Therapy
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.

articles.title_orig: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.title_zh: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.content_orig:
The United States is finalizing a new round of tariffs against China, the EU, and a dozen other countries accused by the Department of Commerce of harming U.S. industry by subsidizing their domestic manufacturers, according to The Wall Street Journal . This is the latest move by the Trump administration to fully restore the trade wall that the president erected on April 2 of last year with indiscriminate tariffs on the entire world, but which were overturned by the Supreme Court.
Several U.S. media outlets are expecting U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to announce the results of the tariff investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 this week. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has been analyzing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favor surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms the U.S. industry. Greer’s team is investigating alleged industrial aid from China, the European Union, and 14 other countries.
The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court’s setback . The court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies because it considered that Trump had exceeded his authority by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to approve tariffs, when this law did not authorize him to do so.
After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labor; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. The latter is expected to be approved soon.
The new tariff will be added to the one approved last July , which affected nearly a hundred countries, including EU members, for allegedly violating forced labor import rules. However, it is being challenged in court.
The federal administration has not disclosed how much the new customs duties will amount to, but they will be similar to those Trump set earlier last year. In any case, they will not exceed the levels set in trade agreements and will be applied specifically to each economy, rather than imposed as a general rate, according to Bloomberg.
It is expected that countries and blocs that signed trade agreements with the United States, such as Japan or the EU, will receive special treatment so that the new tariff complies with the agreements. It is therefore anticipated that tariffs will be 15% or less. Other countries, however, would be set higher tariffs.
China could receive a higher tariff, as the Trump Administration has emphasized that its production subsidies are widespread and particularly harmful to the global economy. Moreover, this would counter criticism arising from the Nvidia case that the White House has been too lenient with China.

articles.title_orig: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
articles.title_zh: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
articles.content_orig:
A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network’s build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket .
The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA’s Vulcan rocket, Amazon’s primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone.
The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight.
Amazon cast a wide net when it started signing deals for launch services five years ago, securing rides on 108 flights with every available medium- or heavy-lift rocket in the West to place a fleet of 3,232 satellites into low-Earth orbit. As of Tuesday, Amazon and its launch partners have completed 17 of those flights, with one mission failure.
Amazon executives initially bought up capacity from US-based United Launch Alliance, Europe’s Arianespace, and Blue Origin. Nearly all of those launch contracts depended on rockets still in development: ULA’s Vulcan, Europe’s Ariane 6, and Blue Origin’s New Glenn.
Each launch vehicle faced development delays, as all new rockets do. New Glenn has been grounded since May after an explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in Florida. ULA’s Vulcan will be sidelined for months after misfiring during a mission with Amazon satellites on November 15.
Amazon started booking launches in 2023 with SpaceX. Falcon 9 successfully launched Amazon’s first three missions last year, each with 24 satellites. Amazon soon reserved 10 more flights on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket as delays mounted with Amazon Leo’s other launch providers, especially ULA and Blue Origin.
The relationship between Amazon and SpaceX is a peculiar one. Amazon aims to catch up to SpaceX’s Starlink network, now boasting more than 11,000 satellites, to bring competition to the satellite broadband market. Federal regulators approved Amazon Leo’s second-generation constellation earlier this year, an addition that will bring the fleet to more than 7,000 satellites in the 2030s. Amazon also plans a direct-to-device service, joining SpaceX and others in the pursuit of consumer demand for mobile connectivity.
But Starlink is far ahead. SpaceX has repurposed the Starlink satellite design for use on several US military programs, and Starlink launches on Falcon 9 are winding down as SpaceX’s Starship enters service . Starship is capable of launching heavier, more powerful Starlink satellites, a culmination that will only widen the gap with Amazon and other competitors in the satellite Internet business.
Starlink’s move to Starship opens up launch slots on Falcon 9, allowing Amazon to accelerate its launches with SpaceX in the near term. But SpaceX doesn’t plan to keep Falcon 9 around for long. The company has reportedly stopped accepting commercial Falcon 9 bookings after 2028.
That means Amazon Leo needs its other launch providers to step up. Arianespace is doing so, with four successful Ariane 6 flights for Amazon this year. Amazon reserved six additional flights with Arianespace in September as Ariane 6 proved its mettle.
But there are questions about Europe’s ability to ramp up production of Ariane 6 rockets, which are single-use and not reusable like Falcon 9 and New Glenn. Europe’s rocket factories are sized to support a launch cadence of up to nine or 10 Ariane 6 flights per year. Arianespace will likely reach six Ariane 6 flights this year, with one more remaining before the end of December.
European taxpayers paid for development of the Ariane 6 and the industrial capacity to build the rockets, and they continue to subsidize each Ariane 6 flight, whether it carries a European government payload or commercial satellites for a large American corporation like Amazon.
European government ministers are mulling proposals to increase Ariane 6 production to meet surging demand from commercial users and Europe’s internal space programs. A decision could come next month , but a ramp-up in launch cadence won’t happen overnight.
Amazon paid United Launch Alliance hundreds of millions of dollars for expansion at Cape Canaveral, Florida, to prepare for as many as 25 Vulcan launches per year. Such a launch cadence is a long way off for ULA, which has now launched Vulcan five times (with one failure) in its three years of service.
Blue Origin, owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, could resume New Glenn flights early next year after completing a launch pad rebuild. It is not clear when Amazon might begin launching on New Glenn, but finding slots in the rocket’s launch schedule could be difficult as Blue Origin prioritizes work for NASA’s Artemis lunar program.
In the meantime, SpaceX will offer Amazon its most assured rides to space. Falcon 9s can launch from Cape Canaveral every few days, and Amazon is ready to tap into that capability with hundreds of satellites in storage waiting to go to orbit.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo ship struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland has left Finnish territorial waters after posing a “serious danger” there, according to Finland’s President Alexander Stubb.
Stubb said late on Sunday that Finland would continue working to maintain stability and security in the Gulf of Finland and thanked the authorities for their response to Saturday’s incident.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it was previously anchored. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
A fire aboard the Sparta II continued to burn through the night despite efforts to extinguish it, the Finnish coastguard said.
“Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” Stubb said on X.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to United States sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_zh: Micron Stock Is Counting on a Buyback Bounce. Why It’s No Slam Dunk.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Shares of Nvidia fell 5% in premarket trading on Tuesday after a 31.2% surge on news that founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as CEO. That came just 12 days after he resigned amid a personal scandal and federal chip-export probes.
Interestingly, AMD shares rose 6.3% yesterday — a telling move that investors continue to believe in the AMD story.
It's a good story to buy into.
CEO Lisa Su — Yahoo Finance's 2026 CEO of the Year award winner — surprised everyone by spending $8.2 billion to scoop up World Labs , gaining a true AI innovator that focuses on software for 3D environments.
World Labs was founded in 2024 and is led by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher known in tech circles as the "Godmother of AI." She was once the chief scientist at Google Cloud ( GOOG ).
Just a few weeks ago, AMD delivered a strong double beat in its third quarter earnings report. Third quarter sales jumped 45% year over year to a record $13.38 billion, comfortably surpassing Wall Street consensus estimates of roughly $13.06 billion.
Adjusted earnings climbed 74% to $2.09 per share, easily topping analyst projections of $1.94 per share.
The blowout performance was anchored by AMD's Data Center segment, where revenue surged 97% to a record $8.5 billion on robust demand for EPYC server processors and the production ramp of Instinct MI450 AI accelerators.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it sees 50% sequential growth in data centers. In 2027, Su guided to revenue growing more than 80%, with server revenue doubling and data center AI more than doubling.
Amid a year of impressive earnings execution, AMD also unveiled its next-generation AI chips, headlined by the Instinct MI450 Series GPUs and the 6th Gen EPYC Venice CPUs. The new chips are designed to power AMD's new Helios rack-scale AI systems , which combine GPUs, CPUs, networking, and software into an integrated platform for training and running large AI models.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) said it began deploying Helios across Azure AI services in the second half of 2026.
The company also announced a major tie-up with Anthropic ( ANT ), significantly expanding its push to challenge Nvidia in the AI infrastructure market.
Anthropic plans to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of the Instinct MI450 GPUs in its Helios system beginning in the first half of 2027 — a deal that could be worth tens of billions of dollars over time. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, marking one of the chipmaker's largest strategic investments ever.
The biggest thing to watch, experts say, is how a hungry-to-prove-himself Huang executes on new chip designs over the next five to seven years. If Huang unlocks an epic gear on the design front, then the entire chip space could be in trouble from a market share perspective.
"Jensen will be on a mission," EMJ Capital founder Eric Jackson said on Sozzi Unleashed .
For now, though, AMD is still in the AI game in a big way.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.title_zh: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.content_orig:
Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi , as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”
However, on Tuesday, Utah decided to drop the criminal charges against Kalshi, McGavick confirmed to Ars. In a statement on X, Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth said, “We are pleased that Utah has chosen to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi, while proceeding with civil litigation. Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized. We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”
In a press release , Brown explained that the charges were dropped specifically due to the pause.
“Kalshi said it would geofence Utah, which blocks access to its site in the state,” the press release said. “The company also committed to monitor for Utah-based IP addresses trying to reach its site. The Office then reevaluated its position and moved to dismiss the criminal case against the company and the individual defendants.”
Brown threatened that the charges would be raised again if Kalshi tried to renew operations.
“Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Brown said. Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every company in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”
Discussion of the Kalshi pause in a Utah sub-Reddit found some Redditors skeptical of the state’s cases as potentially overreaching.
However, many top commenters seemed pleased with the enforcement efforts, suggesting that Utah may have bipartisan support among some residents. One commenter cheered on the attorney general’s efforts as “the one item in the Utah GOP’s agenda I can get behind,” while another agreed that “prediction markets are incredibly toxic and are manipulated against ordinary people.”
Many complained that Kalshi ads flooded their social media feeds. Some suggested the state should focus on banning advertising of prediction markets, while potentially still allowing adults to trade on event contracts if they want to throw their “money away.”
Fears of insider trading were also raised. One commenter laid out why prediction markets seem suspiciously designed to promote insider trading and other market manipulation:
“I’m pretty libertarian and hate banning things. But gambling and prediction markets are a scourge. Even the term ‘prediction market’ is a misnomer. Because ultimately when people with big dollars get involved it creates a financial incentive for them to make fucked up things happen in the real world. Think about it, decades ago we understood that sports betting was a problem because it corrupted sports—s omething that ultimately is pretty meaningless. Then we got all these people betting on the stock market with puts and it created huge incentives to cause havoc with markets. Now if people are betting big money on politics and wars and everything else, it just means people with influence can make money by making improbable/unexpected things happen.”
One commenter joked, “I wonder how Kashi would have reacted if the judge in charge of their case had ‘traded’ $500,000 on the event of them losing the case. Not a problem at all, right?”
On the same day Kalshi announced its temporary pause in Utah, a judge rejected a request from New York Attorney General Letitia James to immediately shut down Kalshi in that state, Courthouse News reported .
New York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane said she was “uncomfortable” granting the temporary restraining order so early in the case because “there does seem to be an indication that there would be market disruption that I’m concerned about.” Kalshi attorney Grant Mainland described it a little differently, claiming that a sudden halt would cause a “market emergency.”
“I think this is the ultimate relief in the case, which is improper for me to do without full briefing,” Crane said. Instead of granting James’ request, she recommended that Kalshi take steps to address the state’s top concerns by considering “safeguards for users between 18 and 20,” who are under the state’s legal gambling age, Courthouse News reported.
According to Kalshi’s estimates, New York’s Kalshi user base (1.5 million) is much larger than Utah’s, so the market disruption from the Utah shutdown may not have carried the same dire stakes for Kalshi or its broader user base.
The CFTC has sought to intervene in that case, too, and it seems clear that Kalshi expects the questions of who can regulate prediction markets and what trading qualifies as a “bet” to reach the Supreme Court. Kalshi’s spokesperson did not respond to Ars’ questions on how the Utah pause broadly impacted users or the platform.
So far, “three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate prediction markets, while a fourth found they cannot,” Courthouse News reported. But despite the current balance tipping toward allowing states to regulate prediction markets, Kalshi appears confident that the Supreme Court will resolve the disparate court rulings in its favor.
In a lawsuit filed by a disgruntled Kalshi user, Kalshi argued that it would waste lower courts’ time to continue litigating these cases and that no case should be resolved until the Supreme Court weighs in.
In that case, Kalshi user Scott Bright alleged that he lost more than $300,000 on sports bets that were technically illegal in Washington.
According to Kalshi, all of Bright’s claims rest “on the premise that state gambling laws reach KalshiEX’s federally regulated exchange—the question now before the Supreme Court. Plaintiff puts the cart before the horse; Defendants ask only that the Court let that threshold question be resolved first.”
The court has yet to address Kalshi’s request to stay the case, but Bright has argued that Kalshi is trying to “sideline a case governed by binding Ninth Circuit precedent so that they can wait for a Supreme Court decision that may never come.”
Kalshi did not respond to Ars’
