articles.title_orig: Nixon had a tell when he lied. His lawyer told Bob Woodward all about it.
articles.title_zh: Nixon had a tell when he lied. His lawyer told Bob Woodward all about it.
articles.content_orig:
Author and investigative journalist Bob Woodward at his home in Washington on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. J. Scott Applewhite/AP hide caption
For more than half a century, Bob Woodward entered people's lives as they rose to power and left behind his draft of history.
"I think I've never ended an interview," Woodward told Morning Edition . There were always more questions to ask.
Now, at 83, he's answering some questions about himself — the experiences that shaped him, the decisions he made as a journalist and what he might have gotten wrong.
Woodward is the reporter who, with Carl Bernstein, exposed the Watergate scandal that brought down President Richard Nixon. He has written revelatory books about presidents ever since.
In his new book, Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir , released Tuesday, Woodward turns his attention to the secrets of his own life. A broken family. Chance encounters that changed his career. Sources who trusted him. Stories he didn't get right.
After 55 years at The Washington Post , he also reflects on what it takes to do good journalism — and what stands in its way today.
The reporter also chooses to reveal some of the anonymous sources who gave him information — a decision that raises ethical questions about protecting confidential sources after their deaths.
"I thought this was a time to let people know. And these are people who didn't do bad things. Actually, they were people who were trying to get the true story out," Woodward said.
In some cases, the sources are dead now. In others, they gave permission.
It's common in Washington to think that people who feed reporters information get better coverage, though some of Woodward's books complicate that idea.
His book about Bill Clinton's administration described a chaotic and dysfunctional White House. Looking back decades later, Woodward says he missed a larger story: the peace and prosperity of Clinton's presidency.
"I didn't see that at the time, and that's my fault," he said.
In the run-up to the Iraq War, Woodward buried in the 16th paragraph of a story an admission from Bush administration officials that they had no smoking gun on Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction.
"That should have been the lead," he said.
Journalists Carl Bernstein, second from left, and Bob Woodward, second from right, are flanked by actors Dustin Hoffman, left, and Robert Redford, right, at the premiere of All the President's Men in Washington on April 5, 1976. AP hide caption
In the memoir, Woodward recalls how he and Bernstein could spend two or three weeks on a single story during Watergate. He worries that the internet has fostered a culture of impatience at the expense of in-depth reporting.
"The secret to impactful reporting is time," he writes.
Woodward also criticizes Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos for remaining silent on President Trump's attacks on the press, while noting that, to his knowledge, Bezos has not interfered in the newspaper's news operation.
"An owner is supposed to be a custodian of uncompromising reporting," Woodward writes.
Woodward traces his investigative reporting back more than 70 years to when he was a child in Wheaton, Ill.
"My family was fracturing right before me. My mother ran off with my father's best friend," Woodward told Morning Edition .
He found out about his parents' divorce by looking in his father's sock drawer.
"Find the sock drawer and look there," he said.
Woodward became a reporter after serving in the Navy. He says he was accepted to Harvard Law School and turned that down to work for a weekly newspaper. His father, a lawyer and a judge, told him: "You're crazy."
What is so great about being a reporter that he wanted to do it?
"That you get to make momentary entries into people's lives when they're interesting, and then get the hell out when they cease to be interesting, which is what always happens," Woodward said.
Woodward came by NPR's studios accompanied by an aide who held a cane in case he needed it.
As technology transforms journalism and the pressures on reporters mount, Woodward's approach to reporting remains rooted in human connection.
"I will continue to show up and knock on doors, even with a cane in my hand," he writes in the book's closing pages.
Later today, you can watch our extended video conversation with Bob Woodward exclusively in the NPR app. You'll find it in the "Video" tab. And if you don't have the app, download it now at npr.org/gettheapp .
The radio interview was edited by Adriana Gallardo. The digital version was produced by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
A previous web description for the audio version of this story incorrectly referred to Bob Woodward's memoir as Secrets: A Reporting Memoir. The title is Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir .
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:

Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."

articles.title_orig: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.title_zh: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.content_orig:
President Donald J. Trump has accomplished something extraordinary. He directly inserted himself into the boardroom of one of America's most strategically important companies, Nvidia , helping to reverse a corporate leadership decision, and personally vouched for restored CEO Jensen Huang as having a clean bill of health regarding the national security investigations into his business activities with China.
On Monday, after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang following his resignation amid a counterintelligence controversy and allegations that Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, is under suspicion of being a Chinese intelligence asset, Wall Street celebrated with a historic market bounce. But the market's enthusiasm should not obscure a far more consequential question circulating in Washington, D.C.: Does American national security have a price?
What happened at Nvidia raises the frightening possibility that it does, and it fits a recent pattern that is exactly what geopolitical rivals around the world want to see. Consider the economic pressures surrounding the Iran war. Disruptions to energy markets, shipping, supply chains, and consumer prices have complicated American strategic decision-making. These are notably different circumstances, but they raise the same troubling question about the costs of defending American national security interests, and when they become economically unpalatable to those in the Trump administration.
Beijing, Tehran, and Moscow are watching — as are our allies and partners — and they all may agree on one thing: America has an Achilles' heel that military and technological superiority cannot overcome. It is possible to impose sufficient economic pain to alter Washington's strategic calculation with friends and foes alike. Bleed American capital markets, disrupt commerce, squeeze consumers, and eventually Washington may look for an exit.
Despite the narrative that the president is weaving, there is a fundamental difference between responsibly weighing economic consequences and allowing adversaries to conclude that they can impose an economic veto over U.S. national security policy. Trump told CNBC in an extensive interview on Monday morning that when it comes to national security, "losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen ... would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about."
"The bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was you know he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "This was a big loss. This was a tremendous loss. And you saw that it affected the market. It affected even, I think it even affected the perception of our country in the world," the president said.
And that's true, but not only in the way Trump thinks it did.
This is not about whether Huang is a brilliant executive or whether Nvidia is enormously important to American competitiveness. Both are true. The question that America, particularly its government, must ask is whether Huang's economic importance justifies subordinating corporate governance, interfering with counterintelligence procedures, and stymying national security oversight.
Trump characterized the Justice Department's assessment as having exonerated Huang. Yet Nvidia's board reinstated him while its own review remained open.
The allegations involving reported contacts with Chinese intelligence assets do not establish legal wrongdoing. However, presidential personal assurances are not substitutes for independent counterintelligence assessments and investigations or congressional oversight. Monday's rising stock price might only measure what shareholders believe Huang at the helm of Nvidia is worth, while discounting or ignoring the unresolved counterintelligence risk that Huang may still pose to Nvidia and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem.
The Trump administration, Silicon Valley, and Wall Street may believe the matter is closed.
"That thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taking the whole market," Trump told CNBC about Nvidia's 31.5% Monday gains.
One glaring vulnerability still on the horizon is what Washington does not know. If Beijing possesses additional damaging information, it controls whether, when, and how that information might be weaponized in an ongoing and now reignited strategic competition between the U.S. and China. Beijing retains the capacity to reopen this matter at a time of its choosing. Chinese intelligence could drip-feed disclosures, compel repeated explanations from Huang and the president, and transform Monday's declaration of resolution of this matter into a prolonged national security vulnerability.
There is also a striking irony here. Some pundits are comparing Trump's intervention to China's state-controlled market. To be sure, the Chinese government has a very heavy hand in its economy, but one thing the Chinese Communist Party will never do is put an individual ahead of national security and political authority despite the economic impact that this person or company is perceived to have. Xi Jinping and China's Communist Party have demonstrated a willingness to make almost the opposite calculation about national security and economic growth. Under Xi, national and political security generally takes precedence over the interests of individual companies and brilliant executives.
Consider Jack Ma. In 2020, Beijing halted Ant Group's planned $37 billion initial public offering and subsequently imposed sweeping regulatory restrictions on Ma's business empire. Beijing accepted substantial economic consequences to reinforce national security and political authority. This is not an argument for importing China's authoritarian model into American corporate governance. But the strategic asymmetry is noteworthy to revisit in this latest comparative context. Beijing has demonstrated that even its most celebrated entrepreneurs are not indispensable to the party and the nation. Washington risks signaling that some of its entrepreneurs are in fact indispensable to the state, which ironically potentially makes them even bigger intelligence targets for foreign adversaries.
As an economic matter, the commercial realities of Nvidia's China business make this situation even more perplexing. China, including Hong Kong, accounted for just 9.1% of Nvidia's reported global revenue in fiscal 2026, down from 19.2% the previous year. Its latest fourth-quarter guidance assumes no Chinese data center compute revenue. Nvidia did change the way it reports geographic sales, to customer headquarter address, in late 2025. But anyone familiar with Chinese strategic documents, including the 15th Five-Year Plan, should understand that Beijing has no intention of becoming permanently "addicted" to American chips. Its objective is technological self-reliance, not expanding Nvidia's market share and by extension its dependency on them.
Whatever the exact figure, I cannot think of a number that is worth selling out U.S. national security over, but it certainly isn't  9.1%, which is also a number that will continue to shrink. Furthermore, if the AI ecosystem is critical to our economy and our national security, then selling advanced chips to China or loosening export controls is the opposite of what we should be doing because the chips are used to juice the compute of Chinese LLMs that compete with ours, and to increase the effectiveness and lethality of Chinese weapons systems. The questionable sales of Nvidia chips in Asia, which are at the heart of this story, support neither our economy nor our national security. They undermine them both.
There is also an extraordinary corporate governance precedent that extends well beyond Nvidia and Huang, one that is escalating and growing more bold at each turn. While Trump has intervened in the markets before, in cases including U.S. Steel and Intel , he ha

articles.title_orig: Waymo says recall prompted by 11 new incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes
articles.title_zh: Waymo says recall prompted by 11 new incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes
articles.content_orig:
Alphabet -owned Waymo said Tuesday its new recall of nearly 4,500 self-driving vehicles in the U.S. was prompted by 11 incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes since Oct. 1, including three on a single day this month.
On Friday, Reuters first reported Waymo was issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Last week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on U.S. freeways ​after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state.
Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in a filing released Tuesday that three Waymo vehicles entered freeway lanes marked with cones as closed for construction on Nov. 9, just three days after the company "updated the approved scope of operation to reduce exposure to closed freeway lanes."
Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events, adding it is still working ​on the recall remedy.
The California ban, ​which took effect this month, resulted from a series of incidents in which Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said.
In June, Waymo issued a similar recall for nearly 3,900 robotaxis that drove past ramp closure signs into pre-planned freeway construction zones or entered freeway lanes with active construction by driving between cones.
The ‌manual ⁠traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better respond to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a May 8 collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on Nov. 6.
Earlier this month, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of its robotaxis passing ​stopped school buses.
Separately, NHTSA and the ​National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child who ran into a street in Santa Monica, California.

articles.title_orig: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.title_zh: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.content_orig:
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson said, as the government said she can only return through extradition.
Hasina went into exile in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule.
She was later sentenced to death by a Bangladesh court in her absence for ordering the deadly crackdown on the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Announcing her plan to return on the anniversary of the end of her country’s 1971 liberation war with Pakistan , she urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national airline.
“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement on Tuesday.
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, Prime Minister Rahman’s press secretary, told the Associated Press news agency that the government would stick to its position on Hasina’s extradition as a convict.
“My government’s stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
Hasina is expected to be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.
The judiciary had earlier said that Hasina would not be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline and there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.
The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced Hasina from power.
Hasina’s father led the war against Pakistan and after independence was the first leader of the new People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
He was killed in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived as they were out of the country.

articles.title_orig: Chinese media hail Huang’s Nvidia return with warning over ‘witch-hunts’
articles.title_zh: Chinese media hail Huang’s Nvidia return with warning over ‘witch-hunts’
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers a keynote address at the COMPUTEX 2024 conference in Taipei, Taiwan, on June 4, 2024. China is not interested in relying on Nvidia’s semiconductor chips for much longer, writes Jeff Smith. (Shutterstock/Jamesonwu1972)
Does China desperately want to obtain more advanced US semiconductor chips ? Or does it desperately want to keep them out of the country? If you answered “both,” you’d be correct.
Shortly before Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO in the wake of reporting about his affair with a Chinese executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of funneling Nvidia chips to China, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey weighed in. Luckey argued that China was happy to see Huang resign because he was a major advocate for chip sales to China, and Beijing doesn’t want Nvidia selling its chips to Chinese firms.
Luckey is half right. On whether to buy Nvidia chips, the Chinese government is torn between competing factions.
Some actors in China’s tech sector—namely national champion and chipmaker Huawei —want to keep US chips out of the Chinese ecosystem so Chinese software firms are forced to buy domestic Huawei chips. On the other hand, Chinese technology and AI firms like Tencent and ByteDance , or Moonshot and DeepSeek , urgently need more Nvidia chips.
Although Huawei chips are gaining ground, US chips remain more powerful, more reliable, and more abundant. By one informed estimate, Nvidia alone will produce roughly 25 times Huawei’s computing power in 2026.
Huawei admitted in September it cannot yet make enough AI chips to meet demand at home , let alone pursue a major global expansion plan. For Chinese software firms to remain competitive with their world-class counterparts in America, they still need Nvidia chips.
The push and pull of these two competing factions has put the Chinese government in a bind. Its approach can at times appear confusing, incoherent, or contradictory. Since mid-2025, Beijing has alternately blocked and allowed Nvidia chips, sometimes within weeks.
Ultimately, Beijing’s heart is with Huawei, the national champion. Building self-reliance in semiconductor manufacturing is a top Chinese Communist Party (CCP) priority, and pleading for chips from Washington is politically embarrassing for Beijing. This is why keeping China “ addicted ” to US chips over the long term was never a viable strategy.
However, Beijing also knows a full cutoff now could be catastrophic. The Institute for Progress (IFP) estimates that US chips now supply about two-thirds of the AI compute available to Chinese entities: 18 percent bought legally, 22 percent smuggled, and 23 percent rented in overseas data centers. Without smuggled and rented Nvidia chips, China’s leading AI labs would be left in the dust by their American rivals.
While the United States, China, and Russia outclass other powers, they lack the reach to divide the world into spheres of influence.
If nothing else, the US-China-Russia summit showed just how irrelevant international governance institutions have become.
Returning the thousands of Ukraine’s kidnapped sons and daughters should have a more prominent place in US-Russia policy.
The Chinese government has sought to navigate these competing tensions with a balancing act: phase out Nvidia chips from China over the long term while protecting Chinese firms’ access to Nvidia chips through smuggling and offshore data centers in the short term.
It’s a two-track strategy. At home, the market is mostly reserved for Huawei chips and for inference. For the more intensive work of training AI models, Beijing keeps three channels to Nvidia open.
1. Capped legal imports. The Chinese government approves limited Nvidia chip purchases case by case and caps them . By August 2026, ByteDance and Tencent had each purchased about 10,000 Nvidia H200 chips .
2. Remote Access . Beijing has allowed Chinese technology firms to sign multiyear, multibillion-dollar contracts to access Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian data centers. These contracts could not proceed without the CCP’s acquiescence. They now account for a substantial portion of the compute available to Chinese AI firms.
3. Smuggling. IFP estimates that about 1 million H100-equivalent Nvidia chips will have been smuggled into China by the end of 2026. One smuggling scheme alone allegedly moved about $2.5 billion of Nvidia-powered servers to China in 2024–2025. Restricted Nvidia servers are openly advertised in Shenzhen , and Chinese universities have bought restricted servers under official procurement contracts . It strains credulity to argue that this is all happening against the will of the CCP.
New reporting suggests Beijing is doing more than looking the other way. The New York Times reports that China’s Ministry of State Security has run a campaign for at least two years to help Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips, led by a team reporting directly to the minister.
China’s two-track strategy only works if the Nvidia track stays open. Amid the fallout from the Jensen Huang affair, Washington is beginning to close it. A new rule issued by the Commerce Department on November 16—“ written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council ”—will substantially curtail Chinese firms’ access to overseas Nvidia compute.
After the rule was issued, Tencent President Martin Lau said “ everyone is actually having less compute ,” and training timelines for Tencent’s next models would probably slip. Alibaba said the rules could affect its global data center expansion.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s new leadership says it is “ no longer shipping ” chips directly to China, including the H200.
Smuggling rings are also now under greater scrutiny. The Megaspeed criminal investigation and the Super Micro smuggling indictment have Chinese buyers fearing a broader crackdown. Traders are reportedly stockpiling restricted chips ahead of tougher enforcement .
Palmer Luckey was right about Beijing’s goal of long-term self-reliance. But it’s wrong to assume the smuggling is happening against the Chinese government’s will . Beijing isn’t merely tolerating the smuggling: its spy agency is reportedly helping.
A day after Commerce issued its November remote access rule , Beijing threatened countermeasures and called the rule “ economic coercion .” A government that truly wanted Nvidia out of its ecosystem would have welcomed a rule that does the job for it. Beijing protested because the rule closes a channel its own policy depends on.
The back door to Beijing is starting to close, but it isn’t shut yet. That needs to change.
Jeff M. Smith is director of The Heritage Foundation’s Asian Studies Center. He is the editor of Asia’s Quest for Balance: China’s Rise and Balancing in the Indo-Pacific (2018) and author of Cold Peace: China-India Rivalry in the 21st Century (2014). His writing on Asian security issues has appeared in Foreign Affairs , The Wall Street Journal , Foreign Policy , the Harvard International Review , Jane’s Intelligence Review , The National Interest , and The Diplomat , among others. Smith formerly served as the director of Asian Security Programs at the American Foreign Policy Council.
While the United States, China, and Russia outclass other powers, they lack the reach to divide the world into spheres of influence.
If nothing else, the US-China-Russia summit showed just how irrelevant international governance institutions have become.
Returning the thousands of Ukraine’s kidnapped sons and daughters should have a more prominent place in US-Russia policy.

articles.title_orig: The Trump team is getting more and more evasive about Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: The Trump team is getting more and more evasive about Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
When Jensen Huang was shockingly reinstalled as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, both Nvidia’s board of directors and President Donald Trump cast it as the result of the administration’s assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk and faced no legal jeopardy.
But pretty much ever since then, those assurances have appeared less than ironclad.
All of which reinforces what a massive risk both Trump and Nvidia just took , which should be ratcheting up concerns among some very skeptical GOP lawmakers .
The board said in its initial statement Monday morning that its talks with senior government officials left it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk” — despite the fact that he had an affair with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence.
Trump said shortly thereafter on social media that the US government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Trump also said that, despite questions about prohibited Nvidia chips making their way to China, Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
But other officials have yet to publicly double down on those assurances. And Blanche was rather evasive in an interview Monday night. Even Trump has repeatedly emphasized very real caveats.
In addition to the assurances he offered on Truth Social on Monday morning, Trump in a later CNBC interview claimed the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang .
“They did a study. They did a pretty good investigation,” Trump said. “And they felt that he himself was exonerated. I don’t know what word you want to use.”
The US Commerce and Justice Departments previously said investigators had conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as part of an investigation into whether the Singaporean-based company had been diverting US semiconductors.
But now Blanche is talking around all that, with increasingly evasive comments about what sort of investigations have occurred or been opened — even accusing reporters of “mocking” him by asking the questions.
“What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said at the Justice Department on Tuesday. “The FBI, law enforcement, looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t necessarily become an indictment. It just literally is that it’s looking into things.”
Pressed on whether Jensen Huang had been investigated, Blanche threw the question back at reporters. “What does that mean, had Huang been investigated? For what?”
He went on to say, “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.”
And the night before, when Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked whether Huang had been cleared of being a national security risk and of illegal activity, Blanche never offered a direct answer.
He instead referred to a Wall Street Journal story Ingraham had mentioned in her lead-up, and declined to comment on it. Then he mentioned extensive discussions within the administration — but without ever saying that those discussions had confirmed Huang was in the clear.
Blanche eventually landed on saying: “A lot of thoughtful process by administration officials went into this decision, and the right decision was reached, I believe.”
And perhaps most strikingly, despite Trump’s claim that the DOJ had “exonerated” Huang, Blanche wouldn’t even confirm the DOJ had opened an investigation.
Ingraham asked twice whether the investigation was now closed, and Blanche balked.
“That assumes there’s an investigation that’s open. And I — that’s never been discussed publicly,” Blanche said.
That’s a long way from Trump’s claim about Huang having been “exonerated.”
While Blanche was evasive, others in the administration were non-existent when it came to vouching for Trump’s assurances.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio was a case in point.
It was Rubio who disseminated a memo to senior US officials warning about potential counterintelligence risks posed by Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation).
But on Monday, Rubio said nothing publicly about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
He ignored a CNN reporter’s shouted question about it during a public event with a foreign dignitary.
Maybe that wasn’t the forum for an in-depth answer on the subject. But Rubio would seem to be a hugely significantly witness for Trump’s assurances. And the fact that the administration didn’t put him forward was conspicuous.
And even Trump, later Monday morning in his CNBC interview, qualified his assurances.
When talking about whether Huang might have known about prohibited chips making their way to China, Trump said that “he certainly did not know about it.”
But then he quickly added a less-than-certain caveat, appending “or at least that’s been our very powerful impression.”
Later in the interview, Trump twice qualified his assurances about Huang’s lack of legal liability by saying that “we believe” Huang is in the clear.
“I gave them enough assurance,” Trump added.
He later said: “You can only give the assurance as to what you know. But we feel very strongly that he’s in good shape — very good shape.”
None of these comments preclude something else coming out about Huang.
Perhaps Trump and those around him are indeed very confident that nothing is going to come out to undercut their assurances. But they just won’t completely own those assurances yet.
And Blanche’s evasive interview and Rubio’s lack of comment both suggest this could be a familiar dynamic: Trump coming to a conclusion based upon what he wants to believe, and those around him scrambling to justify and bolster his preferred narrative.
But there seem to be plenty of people bent on learning more. And time will tell how well the administration’s qualified assurances hold up.

articles.title_orig: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.title_zh: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.content_orig:
The government has announced an independent inquiry into allegations rogue landlords in Birmingham are making huge profits by exploiting a housing scheme.
BBC Panorama reported last month that some companies in the city were taking advantage of the Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) system, intended to provide housing along with care and support for vulnerable people.
There have been claims of fraud, crime, poor housing and firms receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but not giving them the support they are meant to.
A government spokesperson said an eight-week investigation would begin immediately, with initial findings and recommendations reported to ministers in the new year.
Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.
The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.
In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.
She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country.
"Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote.
"There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."
SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.
In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them .
Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.
Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.
Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating.
"Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.
The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.
More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.
The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties .
The council introduced controls, requiring SEA providers to submit evidence they were delivering more than minimal care to their tenants.
But a recent internal audit showed the authority could not show the review had been completed for 72% of the claims tested.
At the time the results were published, 12,700 live cases were waiting review, of which around 7,100 had exceeded the six-month limit.
Bosses said a plan was in place to reduce the backlog to zero by the end of the year.
Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review.
"I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said.
"Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."
It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.
An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.
That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.
Tuesday's announcement follows a recent letter to the prime minister from councillors Robert Alden and Ken Wood, demanding urgent intervention.
Campaigners have called for action for years, under both Conservative and Labour governments.
Alden, the councillor for Erdington and leader of the Birmingham Conservative group, said it was right that the government examines "why Birmingham has become the epicentre of this crisis and what must change".
"Residents deserve answers about how this was allowed to happen.
"Vulnerable people placed in badly run accommodation deserve proper support, and neighbourhoods suffering the consequences deserve action."
Charities, residents and politicians told Panorama last month that parts of the system were being exploited.
The programme found property agents drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos offering free rooms, PlayStation consoles and holidays.
Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex, said many vulnerable people were being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords".
Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.
She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit.
"I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said.
"I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation."
She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed.
Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months.
"There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging.
"They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe."
Her second SEA initially looked "amazing" with brand new kitchen appliances and mattresses but Alysha quickly learnt it was not as it appeared.
Managed by a private provider, Alysha said she was promised weekly counselling sessions, access to food banks, and help with GPs.
"But it's not the case, it's not the case at all," she said.
"They're not interested, they come and they just want you to sign that paper to say Alysha's done support this week and that's it."
She added that the home had been left without heating at one point in the winter.
Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA.
The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs.
"There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."
Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need.
But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck".
"I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

articles.title_zh: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.content_orig:
August 27, 2025 (London and Washington, DC) – A major investigation by The Sentry reveals the operations of Russia’s Wagner Group in Mali as a multilayered catastrophe for the people and communities of Mali, for the ruling junta who brought them in, for regional counterterrorism efforts, and for Russia’s brutal strategy for power and natural resource extraction in Africa.
The Sentry’s new investigative report, “ Mercenary Meltdown: The Wagner Group's Failure in Mali ,” details a cascade of operational failures as the mercenary army has become increasingly reactive and violent—"allowing the terrorist groups they were contracted to neutralize gain more control and increase recruitment in Mali.” The report further reveals that the chaotic environment caused by Wagner is generating widening rifts and paranoia within the Malian military leadership.
Justyna Gudzowska, Executive Director of The Sentry , said: “As Moscow spreads its tentacles across the Sahel and rebrands its operations under the Africa Corps umbrella, it is critical to understand that its predecessor—the Wagner Group—was not the infallible fighting force and successful economic actor it pretended to be. If anything, the Malian example illustrates that the group failed on both fronts, and this should be a warning to other African clients who are considering bringing in the Ministry of Defense-backed Africa Corps.”
Wagner’s involvement in Mali presents an altered trajectory for Russian interventions in the region and a contrast to its devastating and lucrative operations in the Central African Republic, detailed in The Sentry’s 2023 investigative report “ Architects of Terror .”
Charles Cater, Director of Investigations at The Sentry , said: “The Wagner Group’s intervention in Mali has been a failure. Heavy-handed and poorly informed counter-terrorism operations have strengthened alliances among armed groups challenging the state, caused substantial battlefield losses for Wagner, and resulted in higher civilian casualties. Wagner’s presence has also increased political fragmentation and tensions within the junta that hired them, while coming at an unsustainably high economic cost. Ultimately, Wagner’s deployment has not served the interests of the people of Mali, the military government, or even the mercenary group itself.”
Oliver Windridge, Senior Advisor for UK and EU at The Sentry , said: “So far, the European Union and its member states have been reacting with alarm to the specter of Russia's encroachment into the Sahel and other African countries. But the European Union may be operating on an outdated understanding of Wagner’s strength and tactics. As the cracks in Wagner's operations have been revealed, alternative options may also be emerging for Brussels, London, and Washington to exert influence with Sahelian leaders toward better outcomes for their countries.”

The Sentry is an investigative and policy organization that seeks to disable multinational predatory networks that benefit from violent conflict, repression, and kleptocracy. Pull back the curtain on wars, mass atrocities, and other human rights abuses, and you’ll find grand corruption and unchecked greed. These tragedies persist because the perpetrators rarely face meaningful consequences. The Sentry aims to alter the warped incentive structures that continually undermine peace and good governance. Our investigations follow the money as it is laundered from war zones to financial centers around the world. We provide evidence and strategies for governments, banks, and law enforcement to hold the perpetrators and enablers of violence and corruption to account. These efforts provide new leverage for human rights, peace, and anti-corruption efforts. Learn more at: https://TheSentry.org

articles.title_orig: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.title_zh: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Anthropic fell 8% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price.
The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.
Anthropic's initial public offering was oversubscribed, and roughly half of the institutional investors that placed orders for the stock were left empty-handed, as CNBC previously reported . But at least for now, as the market wavers, those firms don't appear to be racing to scoop up shares.
Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday.
Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending."
Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target.
"The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.
Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market."
"While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme."
Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock.
They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company.
"While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.content_orig:
July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery
Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.
The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.
A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.
The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.
Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.
The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.
The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.
Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.
Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.
Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.
Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

articles.title_orig: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
articles.title_zh: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
articles.content_orig:
Andrei Chibis's wife rejects the allegations and he is expected to appear in court on Thursday
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.
Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of  more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; Â£9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.
Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.
He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".
In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."
Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.
Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.
The port of Murmansk is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet
Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.
However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.
The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.
Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.
According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.
He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title_orig: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.title_zh: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027
articles.title_zh: No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027
articles.content_orig:
Are you paying a subscription fee for hardware already installed on your car? Not for much longer, you’re not. At least, not if you live in New York. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill prohibiting automakers, dealers, and other third parties from charging subscription fees for vehicle features that use pre-installed components or hardware. Those heated seats you’re paying for? Get ready to cancel that subscription. That remote start you buy each winter? Treat yourself to an expensive latte from that cafe you like instead.
See all results for used cars for sale near 12306
The new law (S.9348A/A.10411A) doesn’t stop automakers from charging subscriptions entirely, but it does stop them from being able to charge recurring payments for hardware that doesn’t cause them any recurring costs.
Hochul’s office specifically pointed to heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving, and entertainment options. Heated seats are pretty cut and dry, but hands-free driving poses an interesting question. Systems such as Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD), GM’s Super Cruise, and Ford’s Blue Cruise all require customers to pay for a subscription to operate. All three systems work with the hardware installed on their respective vehicles, but the automakers could—and likely will—argue that they have recurring costs to keep the systems updated and safe.
Car and Driver reached out to Governor Hochul’s office for clarification on how the law will affect hands-free driving systems. We will update this story if we hear back. Meanwhile, the new law will go into effect on February 27, 2027, giving automakers and third-party companies time to enter into compliance.
Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver . His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration tees up tariff hikes on EU, China, others
articles.title_zh: Trump administration tees up tariff hikes on EU, China, others
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. trade representative's office is set to unveil its latest tariff plans Tuesday night.
The Trump administration will propose new tariff hikes Tuesday night on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan and 12 other trading partners, a major step towards recreating the president’s global duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
According to one person with knowledge of the planning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will announce the new tariff proposals as part of a report into the countries’ excess manufacturing capacity. The findings are the product of a trade investigation Greer’s office launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. trade representative to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices.
Three other people briefed by the administration on the investigation confirmed the report was in the process of being finalized and the results would be announced as soon as today. They were granted anonymity to share details of policy plans that are not yet public.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement was coming.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.title_zh: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.content_orig:
His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.
"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia , saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC .
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S & P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation .
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.
